@Kaiido thank you for the review! I've fleshed things out more, renaming to `drawHTMLElement()` (because `drawElement()` will probably not be workable in WebGL) and adding the `layoutsubtree` attribute.

There's still some handwaving going on of course, in particular what causes the subtree to be laid out but not painted.
I've fleshed this out some more now, in particular the hit testing.
Thanks for the review @progers! I've left two comments unresolved where I'd like more feedback.

> The introduction of the ElementImage interface makes me wonder if the `onpaint` event is the correct route to expose it, though I don't have a better suggestion... Currently it seems that it wouldn't be bound to a particular `OffscreenCanvas`, and thus it's a bit weird to have to wait on this object's `onpaint` event to have access to such object. But I see how having the notification of updates in the worker is a good thing.
> 
> (_thinking aloud_): Maybe the event could fire on the ElementImage object itself, though I can't see the full picture with such an approach...

This isn't really true. A given `<element>` can only be a child of a single `<canvas>` at a given time, so `ElementImage` really is bound to a particular `OffscreenCanvas`. If you try to `drawElementImage` using an `ElementImage` that belongs to a different canvas, the implementation should throw.

As a practical matter, it's common (I believe) to draw a canvas not in bits and pieces but in a single monolithic operation; so it would be inconvenient to have `onpaint` notifications for multiple elements delivered independently. How do you know when you've received the last one?

For these reasons, I think it makes sense to keep this interface canvas-centered.

> This isn't really true. A given `<element>` can only be a child of a single `<canvas>` at a given time, so `ElementImage` really is bound to a particular `OffscreenCanvas`. If you try to `drawElementImage` using an `ElementImage` that belongs to a different canvas, the implementation should throw.

As currently written, the algorithms do not require this and do not imply this either. Each ElementImage holds a reference to its snapshot and only if the snapshot doesn't exist anymore it would throw, but `drawElementImage` when it receives an ElementImage doesn't check where the ElementImage came from, it only gets the referenced snapshot. If this is really the model, then there is no reason to prevent a context from another canvas/OffscreenCanvas to use that ElementImage. If the idea is to limit the usage of the ElementImage to the canvas/OffscreenCanvas where the paint
event fired, then the algos need a refactor.

> As a practical matter, it's common (I believe) to draw a canvas not in bits and pieces but in a single monolithic operation; so it would be inconvenient to have `onpaint` notifications for multiple elements delivered independently. How do you know when you've received the last one?

I agree, it's probably the most common case and the most useful behavior. But then I believe every snapshot should be available in the event and not only the "changed elements". Having to maintain a list from the first frame, with no way to see the ones that are removed seems like terrible DX. Maybe a boolean could be added to the ElementImage interface to signal whether this particular snapshot did change from last frame to handle the case where one would want to only redraw the elements that did actually change.

If you try to `drawElementImage` using an `ElementImage` that belongs to a different canvas, the implementation should throw.
>

Each ElementImage holds a reference to its snapshot and only if the snapshot doesn't exist anymore it would throw, but `drawElementImage` when it receives an ElementImage doesn't check where the ElementImage came from, it only gets the referenced snapshot. If this is really the model, then there is no reason to prevent a context from another canvas/OffscreenCanvas to use that ElementImage. If the idea is to limit the usage of the ElementImage to the canvas/OffscreenCanvas where the paint event fired, then the algos need a refactor.

@progers WDYT? Seems to me like allowing `drawElementImage` into a canvas that is not the DOM ancestor of the element would open a can of worms, and I can't think of why it would be important for developers.

> 
> > As a practical matter, it's common (I believe) to draw a canvas not in bits and pieces but in a single monolithic operation; so it would be inconvenient to have `onpaint` notifications for multiple elements delivered independently. How do you know when you've received the last one?
> 
> I agree, it's probably the most common case and the most useful behavior. But then I believe every snapshot should be available in the event and not only the "changed elements". Having to maintain a list from the first frame, with no way to see the ones that are removed seems like terrible DX. Maybe a boolean could be added to the ElementImage interface to signal whether this particular snapshot did change from last frame to handle the case where one would want to only redraw the elements that did actually change.

We have no intention of keeping around ElementImages for elements that are no longer a `<canvas layoutsubtree>` child. That sounds like a recipe for an epic memory leak. The `HTMLCanvasElement` itself will provide a way to access all currently-valid ElementImages regardless of whether they have changed.

> We have no intention of keeping around ElementImages for elements that are no longer a `<canvas layoutsubtree>` child. 

To be clear, I was proposing to expose all the children as ElementImage in every paint event, rather than only the ones that did change like currently proposed.

Drive-by comment about styling/layout of the contents of a `layoutsubtree` canvas:

Canvas being a replaced element doesn't stop selectors from matching its children; that part already works normally.

It does prevent us from laying out the children, absent instructions on how to do so. I *think* what's expected here is that the elements lay out as normal children of the canvas, with the appropriate containments applied by the UA style sheet, right? Like, the canvas is just an ordinary block container as far as they're concerned. We can just specify that, and further say (already present in the spec) that they don't paint, but they do respond to hit-tests, selections, etc as normal. The element snapshot is then them doing a special paint operation.

Or does each child lay out independently, as if it's the sole child of the canvas, so that when you draw we can just snapshot from the canvas's 0,0 point and place that at the draw location? That works too, it just needs some clarifying text if so.

Can we get a canvas method that renders CSS anchors at (X,Y) positions as shadowdom elements? Then, canvas children just anchor position to their respective points by name and we get to use actual HTML *on* canvas instead of images of HTML *in* canvas? Or is there another use case here that I don't see?

> Can we get a canvas method that renders CSS anchors at (X,Y) positions as shadowdom elements? Then, canvas children just anchor position to their respective points by name and we get to use actual HTML _on_ canvas instead of images of HTML _in_ canvas? Or is there another use case here that I don't see?

Hi @AutoSponge , are you asking why we don't use anchor positioning to move elements on top of the canvas, like https://github.com/shuding/cobe? This is a good question, as this API ultimately does need to keep the DOM synchronized with what is being drawn into the canvas. Our goal with this API is to enable patterns that are just not possible today, such as interleaving canvas drawing commands with html (e.g., [jelly slider](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas?tab=readme-ov-file#live-demo-source-using-the-webgpu-copyelementimage-api-to-draw-a-div-under-a-jelly-slider)). The explainer lists the [use cases](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas?tab=readme-ov-file#use-cases) this API is solving.

In the explainer, what you're calling the `<canvas>` fallback others have used to build the semantic proxy layer (a hack that `<canvas>` never intended) that makes their UI accessible, and claiming there's some accessibility improvement/capability by this proposal. I've tried and I still don't see it. What's the % of scenarios where "fallback" content is perceived or interacted with visually? 

I want to help devs use `<canvas>` but I don't want to see a proliferation of graphical UIs with no concern for accessibility. The explosion of TUIs and "GPU-powered" web interfaces are almost complete garbage for accessibility. If this is purely about putting CSS/browser-rendered content in `<canvas>`, then I'd recommend removing the accessibility claims. If I'm missing something, please help me understand. Thanks.
Is it correct that so far only Chromium has shown intent to ship, or are there responses from Firefox/Webkit/… as well?

> As I said in [#11588 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588#discussion_r3157655662) I still don't quite understand the rational to prevent using an `ElementImage` from another canvas. The sizing issue still does exist even with this limitation: A `<canvas>` can be resized after the `ElementImage` has been generated, the browser tab can be moved to a monitor with a different pixel density, the page can be zoomed in, the element can be detached from the document, etc. So there must be a solution for the sizing issues anyway, and it's really unclear to me why that solution couldn't also handle the case of drawing into another canvas.

`drawElementImage()` requires information from the containing canvas to determine the correct rasterization scale of the content. That canvas information is snapshotted along with the drawn element's paint record during regular rendering updates. Drawing an element into a different canvas poses (at least) two problems:

1. To get the necessary canvas information to compute rasterization scale at the time of invocation, we would need to perform a forced layout. That's a performance pitfall and we got strong pushback from Mozilla on that point.
2. OffscreenCanvas on a worker thread does not have access to the necessary canvas information.

> > As I said in [#11588 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588#discussion_r3157655662) I still don't quite understand the rational to prevent using an `ElementImage` from another canvas. The sizing issue still does exist even with this limitation: A `<canvas>` can be resized after the `ElementImage` has been generated, the browser tab can be moved to a monitor with a different pixel density, the page can be zoomed in, the element can be detached from the document, etc. So there must be a solution for the sizing issues anyway, and it's really unclear to me why that solution couldn't also handle the case of drawing into another canvas.
> 
> `drawElementImage()` requires information from the containing canvas to determine the correct rasterization scale of the content. That canvas information is snapshotted along with the drawn element's paint record during regular rendering updates. Drawing an element into a different canvas poses (at least) two problems:
> 
> 1. To get the necessary canvas information to compute rasterization scale at the time of invocation, we would need to perform a forced layout. That's a performance pitfall and we got strong pushback from Mozilla on that point.
> 2. OffscreenCanvas on a worker thread does not have access to the necessary canvas information.

Oh, here's another one that is probably the big obstacle: the hit testing situation becomes *much* more complicated. I can't even think of a way to handle that sanely.

> To get the necessary canvas information to compute rasterization scale at the time of invocation, 

Why would you need to do that? The snapshot is created from the proper canvas, right before its onpaint event. The necessary info *is* available. We're talking about drawing back the ElementImage, not generating it.

> OffscreenCanvas on a worker thread does not have access to the necessary canvas information.

Why isn't this part of the snapshot?

> Oh, here's another one that is probably the big obstacle: the hit testing situation becomes much more complicated. 

I believe it's fine that this one is broken. For all we know the rendered elements may not exist anymore, and if one decides to use it on another canvas I doubt they'll expect hit testing to match on the source one.

___

And still, how would you handle the case of the source canvas being detached from the document at the time the ElementImage is (re)drawn on the context? Certainly the "necessary info" wouldn't match anymore, right?

> > To get the necessary canvas information to compute rasterization scale at the time of invocation,
> 
> Why would you need to do that? The snapshot is created from the proper canvas, right before its onpaint event. The necessary info _is_ available. We're talking about drawing back the ElementImage, not generating it.

I'm not sure what you mean by the "proper" canvas. The scenario is that `element` is a child of `canvasA` but you want to call `canvasB.drawElementImage(element)`. When the snapshot is created, we collect the necessary information about `canvasA` because it is the DOM parent of `element`. At what point would we collect the necessary information about `canvasB`? We can't know _a priori_ that you intend to call `canvasB.drawElementImage(element)`. I'm using Element and ElementImage interchangeably here, the situation is the same either way.

> > OffscreenCanvas on a worker thread does not have access to the necessary canvas information.
> 
> Why isn't this part of the snapshot?

Information about `canvasA` is part of the snapshot, information about `canvasB` is not.

> > Oh, here's another one that is probably the big obstacle: the hit testing situation becomes much more complicated.
> 
> I believe it's fine that this one is broken. For all we know the rendered elements may not exist anymore, and if one decides to use it on another canvas I doubt they'll expect hit testing to match on the source one.

If you don't care about hit testing or accessibility or interactivity --  if you just want a pixel stamp of an element -- then you can simply: `canvasA.drawElementImage(element); canvasB.drawImage(canvasA)`.

> The scenario is that element is a child of canvasA but you want to call canvasB.drawElementImage(element). 

Ok, so I think that's where the misunderstanding lies, I am not talking about drawing an `Element`, but an `ElementImage`. So the scenario is, that `element` is a child of `canvasA`, I call `canvasA.captureElementImage(element)` to generate `img`, and then I want to call `canvasB.drawElementImage(img)`.  

> ... then you can simply: canvasA.drawElementImage(element); canvasB.drawImage(canvasA).

This implies we dirty the "visible" canvasA, it also converts the drawing ops into pixels, and loses the vector-like resizing feature.

And this solution still does not handle the case of drawing an `ElementImage` on its source canvas, when said canvas is detached.

> > The scenario is, that element is a child of canvasA but you want to call canvasB.drawElementImage(element).
> 
> Ok, so I think that's where the misunderstanding lies, I am not talking about drawing an `Element`, but an `ElementImage`. So the scenario is, that `element` is a child of `canvasA`, I call `canvasA.captureElementImage(element)` to generate `img`, and then I want to call `canvasB.drawElementImage(img)`.

That makes no difference. `captureElementImage()` doesn't do anything special, it just returns a wrapper around information that was generated internally during the rendering update. The only reason it exists is for sending to a worker thread, which cannot be done with `Element`.

> > ... then you can simply: canvasA.drawElementImage(element); canvasB.drawImage(canvasA).
> 
> This implies we dirty the "visible" canvasA, it also converts the drawing ops into pixels, and loses the vector-like resizing feature.

We cannot do vector-like resizing without the information gathered during rendering update.

> That makes no difference. captureElementImage() doesn't do anything special,

What? No, `ElementImage` and `Element` do behave differently: `ElementImage` does hold its snapshot whereas `Element` is just a key to the `<canvas>` live list of snapshots.  
It has to be this way, otherwise doing something like
```js
ctx.drawElementImage(img, x, y);
ctx.drawElementImage(img, x, y);
```
in a Worker could use 2 different snapshots.

> > That makes no difference. captureElementImage() doesn't do anything special,
> 
> What? No, `ElementImage` and `Element` do behave differently: `ElementImage` does hold its snapshot whereas `Element` is just a key to the `<canvas>` live list of snapshots. It has to be this way, otherwise doing something like
> 
> ```js
> ctx.drawElementImage(img, x, y);
> ctx.drawElementImage(img, x, y);
> ```
> 
> in a Worker could use 2 different snapshots.

Well, the premise is faulty because you can never have an Element on a worker thread. But I think this is a moot point; what I really meant is that there is no difference between Element and ElementImage as it pertains to the issue of drawing into a different canvas from the one containing the Element.

> As I said in [#11588 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588#discussion_r3157655662) I still don't quite understand the rational to prevent using an `ElementImage` from another canvas. The sizing issue still does exist even with this limitation: A `<canvas>` can be resized after the `ElementImage` has been generated, the browser tab can be moved to a monitor with a different pixel density, the page can be zoomed in, the element can be detached from the document, etc. So there must be a solution for the sizing issues anyway, and it's really unclear to me why that solution couldn't also handle the case of drawing into another canvas.

When drawing an element from canvasA into canvasB, it is difficult to correctly update the DOM position (transform) of the element so that it matches the on-screen location, which is needed for web platform features like hit testing, accessibility, etc.

> When drawing an element from canvasA into canvasB, it is difficult to correctly update the DOM position (transform) of the element so that it matches the on-screen location, which is needed for web platform features like hit testing, accessibility, etc.

But you face the same issues with an `ElementImage` that holds an out of date snapshot, whether it came from the same canvas or not. The content of the element in DOM may be completely different than what the old snapshot holds (I mean, the original element could even not exist in DOM anymore).  
I personally think it's ok if this is broken, it still allows complex processing using multiple layers and vector sizing, and it's still possible to do the positioning in DOM yourself.  

But if you believe it's a no-go, then there should probably be further limitation to `ElementImage` objects, because only preventing them from being drawn on a different canvas doesn't solve much.

> You can’t have `ElementImage` work as a key over the live map like `Element` does, because in a worker thread you can’t know when the map content in the main thread will change.
> 
> ```js
> canvas.drawElementImage(img, x, y); // uses snapshot_1
> // the map on the main thread is updated, but in the worker we're sync
> canvas.drawElementImage(img, x, y); // uses snapshot_2
> ```
> 
> This shouldn’t happen.

This can never happen, for all kinds of reasons that have nothing to do with HTML-in-canvas. There is no concurrent access of this kind anywhere in JavaScript, with the exception of SharedArrayBuffer. But again -- and I'm having a hard time making myself understood on this point -- the "liveness" of `Element` compared to `ElementImage` is really besides the point...

> Now, this means the “necessary information” from the canvas also needs to be accessible for as long as the `ElementImage` holds it; even if you do maintain a same-canvas policy. You weren’t very explicit about this “necessary information”, but I suppose it would change when the canvas is resized, moved to another monitor or even detached entirely from the document. The current solution provided in the PR, to prevent drawing the `ElementImage` in other canvases, does not solve this issue. You still must keep the “necessary information” along with the `ElementImage` or the snapshot.
> 
> So, if that information is held even for the same-canvas policy, why can’t it be used by another canvas? Why would it work between _canvasA_ and _canvasA-after-a-resize_, but not between _canvasA_ and _canvasB_?

Among the canvas information required to determine the correct raster scale for `drawElementImage()` is the canvas' `width` and `height` attributes, its CSS box size, and its CSS zoom level. All that information is computed for `canvasA` and included in `element`'s snapshot because `element` is a child of `canvasA`. If you call `canvasB.drawElementImage(element)`, we don't have the snapshotted `width`/`height`, CSS box size, and CSS zoom level of `canvasB` available. There are pretty much two options in this situation: do a forced layout to get the necessary information for `canvasB`; or rasterize using the snapshotted information from `canvasA`, which can give screwy results. Maybe you don't care if the raster scale is wrong and you can live with the screwy results; but if that's true then `canvasA.drawElementImage(element); canvasB.drawImage(canvasA)` will work just as well.

As mentioned before, allowing an `ElementImage` to be drawn into a different canvas creates some potentially very confusing situations with respect to hit testing and rasterization scale, and it's very likely to be negative for accessibility as well. It also creates a possible weird loophole for privacy-preserving paint behavior: what should the browser do if you `postMessage` an `ElementImage` to a cross-origin context and draw it into a canvas there?

In my opinion, for all these reasons and for other reasons that I can't even think of right now, your stated reasons for wanting this behavior do not outweight the complexity and potential for confusion.

> This can never happen, ...

I might be wrong, but I'm pretty sure it's still something we defend against when writing cross-context specs.  
Besides, remember we're talking about two JS contexts working in parallel and having access to the same non-JS resources.

> Among the canvas information required to determine the correct raster scale for drawElementImage() is the canvas' width and height attributes, its CSS box size, and its CSS zoom level. 

And that information is gone as soon as the snapshot held by the `ElementImage` object is outdated. So you still face the same issues, even if you allow only drawing on the same canvas.

> It also creates a possible weird loophole for privacy-preserving paint behavior: what should the browser do if you postMessage an ElementImage to a cross-origin context and draw it into a canvas there?

You can also send an `ImageBitmap`, or an `ImageData` of that snapshot rendered on the canvas to that cross-origin context. You can't prevent a page from leaking its data to another page if it wants to do so. What needs to be prevented is the cross-origin doc being able to read that info without the page's consent.  

> canvasA.drawElementImage(element); canvasB.drawImage(canvasA) will work just as well.

Once again, no. This prevents doing complex compositing in a Worker while maintaining the visible canvas clean with the last generated frame for the time the processing is done. It forces you to display an half-baked frame.  

> your stated reasons for wanting this behavior do not outweight the complexity and potential for confusion.

My main point isn't that this should work just for the sake of it, but rather that this limitation doesn't solve anything for an `ElementImage` with an outdated snapshot.

> My main point isn't that this should work just for the sake of it, but rather that this limitation doesn't solve anything for an `ElementImage` with an outdated snapshot.

I sense that we have perhaps reached the limit of what can be resolved with this exchange. If you feel strongly on this point, I'd suggest you file a separate issue to bring it to the attention of the standards bodies. I don't think this PR should be blocked on resolving it.

>  I don't think this PR should be blocked on resolving it.

I think I disagree on this.  
You came as the sole developer of this feature saying that the planned API had an issue. We have to trust you on this, and I do. 
You proposed a solution that does bring some new limitations to the API. This goes against the UX > DX > impl > specs hierarchy, so as a reviewer, I think it's normal I challenge this proposed change. Given this is a whole new API and no actual user has voiced in favor of the particular use cases that would be prevented by this limitation, I do agree it would still be an acceptable change.  

But, even with this limitation, the issue you identified still does exist in some other parts of the API as is shown in [this fiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/mpvwztjy/) (for the green text). This needs to be resolved too. We can't leave the API with a known broken path in it.  
So please provide a solution to also fix the issue you've identified, but for the `ElementImage` objects that point to outdated snapshots,  

From what I gather from your past comments, I am under the impression that it's mainly the magical 3 argument version of `drawElementImage(element, x, y)` that triggers the issue, and that the 5 argument version with explicit `dw` and `dh` wouldn't have the same problem. Is it so? Then maybe, this 3 argument version is the actual problem?

> > I don't think this PR should be blocked on resolving it.
> 
> I think I disagree on this. You came as the sole developer of this feature saying that the planned API had an issue. We have to trust you on this, and I do. You proposed a solution that does bring some new limitations to the API. This goes against the UX > DX > impl > specs hierarchy, so as a reviewer, I think it's normal I challenge this proposed change. Given this is a whole new API and no actual user has voiced in favor of the particular use cases that would be prevented by this limitation, I do agree it would still be an acceptable change.
>

This needs to be resolved too. We can't leave the API with a known broken path in it. So please provide a solution to also fix the issue you've identified, but for the `ElementImage` objects that point to outdated snapshots,
> 
> From what I gather from your past comments, I am under the impression that it's mainly the magical 3 argument version of `drawElementImage(element, x, y)` that triggers the issue, and that the 5 argument version with explicit `dw` and `dh` wouldn't have the same problem. Is it so? Then maybe, this 3 argument version is the actual problem?

This is a known issue with the feature as specified: if you change the canvas grid and draw an outdated `ElementImage` it will have distorted proportions. We went through a very lengthy process of considering [alternatives](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas/blob/main/README.md#alternatives-considered-paint-event-timing) and working with other browsers to find something we all can agree on, and this is it. If you would like to suggest a different approach to the ones already considered please file an [issue](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas/issues) in the project repository. We do not have any clever ideas for how to accomplish this.

In my opinion this is not a significant shortcoming. As a point of comparison: the canvas is already implicitly `clear()`-ed when the canvas grid changes. One could argue that this is also a form of broken-ness -- one which your demo side-steps without complaint by doing all its painting after the resize. As a practical matter developers don't seem to have a problem with it. As for HTML-in-canvas, I don't think it's too onerous to require developers to draw with new element paint snapshots after resizing the canvas grid if they want to avoid distortion. This could perhaps be emphasized in the spec, but I don't agree that this constitutes "broken" behavior.

Specifying `dx/dy` will avoid the behavior but may introduce fuzziness, even if no projection is applied when drawing. Only the three-argument version gives reliably pixel-perfect results when compared to the same content placed outside the canvas.

(Drive by review; I haven't read the full patch or comment history)

Hey folks! I was working on some paint-timing spec cleanup (context: https://github.com/wicg/soft-navigations) and @shaseley pointed out that the "mark paint timing" steps are ambiguously expecting to start pre-paint but end post-paint (i.e., include paint time).

I think your PR nicely clarifies the update-the-rendering steps, but looks like it moves "mark paint time" to come after paint, and would AFAIK change the intent of the `paintTime` value that many specifications rely on for performance reporting.

See: https://github.com/w3c/paint-timing/issues/126

---

I think the best solution would be to split "mark paint timing" into steps that come before paint, and steps that come after.

An alternative solution might be to mark the pre-paint timestamp in update-the-rendering and then pass that timestamp to "mark paint timing", similar to how we mark first, then pass `unsafeStyleAndLayoutStartTime` to "record rendering time".

@foolip , to address @mmocny 's point, we can go ahead and land this "breaking" change that introduces a paint step, and then ask @mmocny to follow up with a change to split paint timing into a pre-paint and post-paint steps, and https://github.com/w3c/paint-timing/issues/126 can track this.

@progers with the structure I'm proposing in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12554 there won't be a definition of "paint" in HTML. I hope that means we can leave this to https://github.com/w3c/paint-timing/issues/126?

Reviewed at 4cfec76. `lint.sh` passes, a full build (including the developer edition) succeeds, and the new external anchors resolve. I compared the text with the explainer, Chromium's implementation, and the tentative WPTs in `html/canvas/{element,offscreen}/manual/draw-element-image/`. Several blockers below are places where those three agree with each other but not with the spec.

**Blockers**

- [The canvas transform has no defined coordinate spaces](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L153954-L153961), and [the `drawElementImage()` formula](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75732-L75739) disagrees with WPT and Chromium. "Applied before CSS transforms" doesn't say what it maps from or to.
  - The explainer, Chromium, and WPT agree that it maps the element's border box, before CSS transforms, into the canvas's content coordinate space. It replaces the layout position and skips the transforms and clips of intervening ancestors.
  - In [canvas-transform-get-bounding-client-rect](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/3280b7aabcd519a65bba4f27e87ed34f50560d85/html/canvas/element/manual/draw-element-image/canvas-transform-get-bounding-client-rect.tentative.html#L39-L45), `translate(50, 60).scale(2, 3)` puts the box at (50, 60) with size 200×150, and [margins don't move it](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/3280b7aabcd519a65bba4f27e87ed34f50560d85/html/canvas/element/manual/draw-element-image/canvas-transform-get-bounding-client-rect.tentative.html#L107-L115).
  - The `T_translate⁻¹·…·T_translate` conjugation only works if the canvas transform is applied around `transform-origin`, which that test rules out. With the default `transform-origin`, `drawElementImage(el, 20, 30, 200, 100)` on a 100×50 element stores `translate(70, 55)·scale(2)`, where Chromium stores `translate(20, 30)·scale(2)`.   - `T_scale` uses the content box. Chromium uses the object-fit/object-position content rect and adds its offset.
  - Without a source rect, Chromium leaves hit testing unclipped, while the spec clips to the border box. (The clip is still an XXX.)

That allows dropping `T_translate`, and with it the snapshot's translation matrix, its comparison, and [the computed value of `transform-origin`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124773-L124775), which can be a percentage.

The text doesn't say whether the element's own `transform`, `opacity`, `filter`, `clip-path`, `mask` or `backdrop-filter` apply, or which ancestor effects do.

  - [nested-drawable-filter](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/3280b7aabcd519a65bba4f27e87ed34f50560d85/html/canvas/element/manual/draw-element-image/nested-drawable-filter.tentative.html#L14-L17) expects a drawable inside a blurred, half-transparent drawable to be drawn without the ancestor's filter and opacity. Chromium reparents effects to the canvas.

- [The layout rules](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L153945-L153963) don't describe a workable layout.
  - Read literally, only the drawable elements themselves are laid out. Their descendants aren't, like the `<span class="val">` in the pie chart. Nor are non-drawable ancestors, like the `<figure>` in the [second example](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L77119-L77123), which CSS needs as containing blocks. Chromium lays out everything under a `content=drawable` canvas.
  - Also missing, compared to the explainer and Chromium: the canvas blockifies its children and forces them to `position: static`, the canvas is a stacking context, and drawables are containing blocks for all their descendants.
  - [`[drawable] { isolation: isolate !important }`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L154038) applies to every element with the attribute, even outside any canvas. Chromium only isolates elements whose nearest canvas is drawable.

- [The drawing step](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75704-L75711) leaves out most of the canvas drawing model.

  - When `sw` or `sh` is 0, [`dw / sw`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75723-L75724) divides by zero. That includes the default for a zero-sized border box ([drawElementImage-zero-size](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/3280b7aabcd519a65bba4f27e87ed34f50560d85/html/canvas/element/manual/draw-element-image/drawElementImage-zero-size.tentative.html#L36-L40)). - [Nested canvases, and same-event-loop iframes, are a frame stale](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124736-L124862).

- Several changes that need a redraw don't fire `paint`:
  - An element that [loses its box](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124767) keeps its old snapshot, because [the cleanup](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124836-L124849) only checks eligibility, and no event fires. [onpaint-remove-drawable-element](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/3280b7aabcd519a65bba4f27e87ed34f50560d85/html/canvas/element/manual/draw-element-image/onpaint-remove-drawable-element.tentative.html#L186-L196) expects one for `display: none`.
  - [Removing the `drawable` attribute](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L86654-L86655) deletes the snapshot synchronously, so the rendering loop never sees it and no event fires. Removing the element does fire one, but only because of the next item.
  - The [pie-chart example](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L77100-L77105) resizes the bitmap from a `ResizeObserver` when the device pixel ratio changes. That clears the bitmap, but every input to the snapshot comparison is in CSS pixels and unchanged. So no event fires and the canvas stays blank. Chromium also compares the device-pixel content box and zoom, and the explainer's `OffscreenCanvas` example calls `requestPaint()` instead.

  Consider the following:
  - drop snapshots of elements without a box in the cleanup loop;
  - set "force paint event" wherever a snapshot is removed outside the rendering loop;
  - set it when a Drawable canvas's bitmap dimensions change, or fix the example.
- [Geometry state isn't cleared](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75888-L75910) when an element stops being eligible. szager said that should happen for any DOM change that makes an element ineligible.
  - DOM runs the removing steps after detaching the node, so [the reset](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L1871-L1872) never finds the canvas. The snapshot and the list-of-drawn-elements entry remain, and nothing prunes that list later. The canvas keeps removed elements alive, and re-inserting one makes it hit-testable before it's drawn. (Fixing this as is would stop the removal `paint` event mentioned above.)
  - Moving steps (`moveBefore()`) and slot or shadow root changes reset nothing. An element moved into another canvas keeps its old transform for layout and accessibility geometry.
  - When drawing an `ElementImage`, the [main-thread branch](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75760-L75767) updates the originating element even if it was collected or is no longer eligible. Chromium checks that the element still belongs to the canvas.
  - [Applying geometry updates](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78134-L78136) checks only the canvas ancestor, not whether the element is drawable.

  Consider keeping the transform, clip, and draw order on the canvas, keyed by element, and ignoring or pruning entries that aren't eligible. At minimum, use _oldAncestor_ and add moving steps.
- With scripting disabled, or in non-visual media, [`content=drawable` content disappears](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L70133-L70136).

So a Drawable canvas that doesn't represent embedded content represents nothing, while [the Drawable rendering rules](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L153939-L153941) still apply. **Suggestions**

- [Positional arguments are omitted in the middle](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75619-L75623). Infra only allows omitting trailing optional positional arguments. The seven-argument overload relies on an HTML comment (`<!-- no dw/dh -->`), so read literally, `sx` binds to `dw`. Consider Infra's named optional parameters, here and for ["with clear set to true"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78044-L78045).
- [The canvas transform and clip](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75913-L75917) are stored as `DOMMatrix` and `DOMRect` objects. In a worker, these are created in the worker's realm and then [assigned to main-thread element state](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78157-L78167). Consider storing a matrix and a rectangle as values, and creating the `DOMMatrix` only in `getElementTransform()`.
- [Garbage collection becomes observable](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75661-L75667): whether drawing throws depends on whether the placeholder `canvas` has been collected. Consider an opaque identifier, as you noted earlier and as Chromium does.
- [`requestPaint()`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L70901-L70905) isn't guaranteed to lead to a `paint` event, because ["Unnecessary rendering"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124524-L124534) only exempts animation frame callbacks. Consider also keeping documents that have a canvas whose "force paint event" is set.
- [The note on amending the prepared rendering](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124864-L124872) says only canvas drawing in `paint` affects the current frame. But the existing step after it still says to "update the rendering … to reflect the current state", which includes DOM changes made by `paint` handlers. Consider having that step present the prepared rendering.
- [`onpaint` and `onelementgeometryupdate`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L126482) are on `GlobalEventHandlers`, so every element and `window` get them, and `onpaint` is a generic global name. Chromium and the explainer put them on `HTMLCanvasElement` only. Consider aligning with that, or confirming compat. The events index also uses [`for="HTMLElement"`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L162347) for one and [`for="HTMLCanvasElement"`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L162478) for the other.
- Consider [`[SameAgentCluster]`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78317) for `ElementImage`; it landed after this PR's base. Its snapshot refers to an element and a canvas that only mean something in the originating agent cluster. The trade-off is an `OffscreenCanvas` transferred to a shared worker.
- [The `canvas` content model](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L70064-L70073) still forbids most interactive content. Even the explainer's basic `<form drawable>` example, with a `label` and an `input`, is non-conforming. Consider relaxing it for the Drawable state.
- A canvas without a box, or with a zero-sized content box, leaves [`canvasWidth`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L124755-L124757) undefined and makes [`scaleX`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L75677-L75682) divide by zero. Consider a guard; Chromium falls back to a scale of 1.
- ["Get the element reference"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L70886-L70887) can't do anything in `getElementTransform()`, whose IDL only takes an `Element`. Consider dropping the step, or accepting `(Element or ElementImage)` like the other methods.
- ["Exposing sensitive information"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78546-L78561) repeats [the paragraph added to the security section](https://github.com/whatwg/html/blob/4cfec766c32b51d85089858bcf7f63bfbe6910f3/source#L78585-L78589), and its heading has nothing under it in the developer edition. Consider dropping it.
